blocks.text: In astronomy, measuring the distances to stars and galaxies is essential for understanding the structure and expansion of the universe.

blocks.title: Standard candles
blocks.text: Standard candles are astronomical objects with known intrinsic brightness (luminosity) that serve as tools for measuring cosmic distances.

blocks.alt: A star at the left sends light into a widening cone. At distances r, 2r and 3r the same beam passes through areas drawn as squares divided into 1, 4 and 9 small squares, labelled F, F/4 and F/9. Below: F = L/(4 pi d^2); standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known luminosity, so measuring F gives d = sqrt(L/4 pi F).
blocks.caption: The inverse-square law and standard candles (original diagram after Figs 21.1 and 21.2).
blocks.long_description: The same power spreads over an area that grows as the square of the distance, so each square metre receives less. Knowing how much power a standard candle emits, the measured flux tells us how far away it is.

blocks.text: By comparing how bright a standard candle appears from Earth (its apparent brightness) with how bright it actually is, astronomers can calculate its distance using the inverse-square law of light: from F = L/(4 pi d^2), d = square root of [L / (4 pi F)]. Examples of standard candles are Cepheid variable stars and Type Ia supernovae, both of which have predictable luminosities that make them reliable distance indicators (Fig 21.2).

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: The idea of standard candles dates back to the 1910s, when Henrietta Swan Leavitt discovered that Cepheid variable stars pulse in a predictable way. Her work laid the foundation for measuring cosmic distances and the scale of the universe.

Two stars appear equally bright. One is a standard candle whose true brightness is well known; the other is not. If the standard candle is farther away, what can you say about the true brightness of the second star?
